# Prologue

Packages we'll use today:


```{r}
if (!require("pacman")) install.packages("pacman")
pacman::p_load(fixest,  tidysynth, tidyverse)
```

Let's load in the German reunification data as well:

```{r}
deu <- haven::read_dta("data/repgermany.dta") %>%
    mutate_at(vars(index, year, gdp, infrate, trade, schooling,
                   invest60, invest70, invest80,
                   industry),
               as.numeric) %>%
    mutate_at(vars(country), as.character)
```

---
# German Reunification

Let's set up our initial synthetic control to replicate [Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12116)

.font80[
```{r}
synth <- deu %>%
    synthetic_control(
      outcome = gdp, # outcome
      unit = country, # unit identifier
      time = year, # time identifier
      i_unit = "West Germany", # treated unit
      i_time = 1990, # treatment year
      generate_placebos = T # whether to generate placebos for inference
    ) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1981:1990, 
                     gdp_81_90 = mean(gdp, na.rm = T),
                     trade_81_90 = mean(trade, na.rm = T), 
                     infrate_81_90 = mean(infrate, na.rm = T)
  ) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1971:1980, 
                     industry_71_80 = mean(industry, na.rm = T)) %>% 
  generate_predictor(time_window =c(1970, 1975), 
                     schooling_70_75 = mean(schooling, na.rm = T)) %>% 
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1980,invest_80 = invest80)
```
]

class: inverse, middle
name: optim

# Optimization Window


---
# Optimization Window

What is the `optimization_window` argument of `generate_weights()` doing if we manually set the time for our predictors?

--

.hi-slate[A: tidysynth] follows Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010) and chooses weights $\nu \in V,\omega \in W$ to .hi-purple[minimize MSPE in the pre-intervention period].

--

By default it does this for the .hi-medgrn[full pre-intervention period] $t= 1,...,\color{#8bb174}{T_0}$:

$$\min_{V,W} MSPE_{t=1}^{\color{#8bb174}{T_0}} = \frac{1}{T_0}\sum\limits_{t=1}^{\color{#8bb174}{T_0}} \left(Y_{1t} - \sum\limits_{j=2}^{J+1}\omega_j(V) Y_{jt}\right)^2$$
---
# Optimization Window


Specifying `optimization_window` as the range $1 \leq \color{#3b3b9a}{t_s},..., \color{#fb6107}{t_e} \leq T_0$ forces only the specified time window to be used when calculating MSPE:

<br>

$$\min_{V,W} MSPE_{\color{#3b3b9a}{t_s}}^{\color{#fb6107}{t_e}} = \frac{1}{\color{#fb6107}{t_e} - \color{#3b3b9a}{t_s} + 1}\sum\limits_{\color{#3b3b9a}{t_s}}^{\color{#fb6107}{t_e}} \left(Y_{1t} - \sum\limits_{j=2}^{J+1}\omega_j(V) Y_{jt}\right)^2$$
<br>

* In the background of the `synth_weights()` function, this is done by filtering the data to `filter(time %in% optimization_window)`

  
---
# Optimization Window: Application

[Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12116), which we're replicating, uses the period 1981-1990 as its optimization window
  * Use 1971-1980 as the training period
  * Use 1981-1990 as the validation period
  * Use predictors in 1971-1980 to build $V$ to minimize RMSPE in 1981-1990
  * Use $V$ to choose $W$ to maximize balance in the decade right before reunification (1981-1990)

---
# Comparing: 81-90 Window

```{r, echo = F}
sc_81_90 <- synth %>%
  generate_weights(optimization_window = 1981:1990) %>%
  generate_control() 

plot_trends(sc_81_90) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 35000))
```

---
# Comparing: 61-90 Window

```{r, echo = F}
plot_trends(sc_61_90) +

```

# Comparing: Pre-Period
 

```{r, echo = F}
sc_path_81_90 <- grab_synthetic_control(sc_81_90) %>%
  rename(synth_y_81_90 = synth_y) %>%
  select(-real_y)
sc_paths <- grab_synthetic_control(sc_61_90) %>%
  rename(synth_y_61_90 = synth_y) %>%
  left_join(sc_path_81_90, by = "time_unit")


ggplot(sc_paths, aes(x = time_unit)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = synth_y_61_90, linetype = "1961-1990")) +
   geom_line(aes(y = synth_y_81_90, linetype = "1981-1990")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = real_y,  linetype = "Actual West Germany"), color = "red3") +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Optimization Window", values = c("1961-1990" = "dashed", "1981-1990" = "solid", "Actual West Germany" = "solid")) + 
scale_y_continuous(name = "Per Capita GDP (PPP current USD)", limits = c(2000, 20500)) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = NULL, limits = c(1960, 1990)) +
  theme_minimal()
```


---
# Comparing: Post-Period


```{r, echo = F}
sc_path_81_90 <- grab_synthetic_control(sc_81_90) %>%
  rename(synth_y_81_90 = synth_y) %>%
  select(-real_y)
sc_paths <- grab_synthetic_control(sc_61_90) %>%
  rename(synth_y_61_90 = synth_y) %>%
  left_join(sc_path_81_90, by = "time_unit")


ggplot(sc_paths, aes(x = time_unit)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = synth_y_61_90, linetype = "1961-1990")) +
   geom_line(aes(y = synth_y_81_90, linetype = "1981-1990")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = real_y,  linetype = "Actual West Germany"), color = "red3") +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Optimization Window", values = c("1961-1990" = "dashed", "1981-1990" = "solid", "Actual West Germany" = "solid")) + 
scale_y_continuous(name = "Per Capita GDP (PPP current USD)", limits = c(20000, 35000)) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = NULL, limits = c(1990, 2003), breaks = seq(1990, 2002, 2)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

---
# Punchline

* Lack of "uniqueness" of synthetic controls (e.g. "local minima")
  * Two different sets of unit/predictor weights
  * Similar pre-treatment fit, post-treatment path
  * Average post-treatment difference between the two SC: $7.97 (0.03% of dependent variable mean)
  
  
```{r, echo = F}
filter(sc_paths, time_unit > 1990) %>%
  mutate(diff = synth_y_81_90 - synth_y_61_90) %>%
  summarise(mean_gdp = mean(real_y),
            mean_diff = mean(diff))
```

name: scaling

# Impact of Variable Scale

---
# Impact of Variable Scale


What if we rescaled one of our variables instead?

Thinking back to our objective function with *just* $Y$ and .hi-red[no other predictors:]

$$\min_{V,W} MSPE_{t=1}^{{T_0}} = \frac{1}{T_0}\sum\limits_{t=1}^{{T_0}} \left(Y_{1t} - \sum\limits_{j=2}^{J+1}\omega_j(V) Y_{jt}\right)^2$$

A rescaled $Y$ *shouldn't* change things, as everything is being scaled equally

---
# Impact of Variable Scale


However, if we instead have a set of multiple predictors, then it .hi-red[should affect things]!

  * Re-scaling $Y$ or $X_k$ changes its proportional representation in the overall squared difference term
    * Ex: a squared difference of inflation rate as percent is 10000 times larger than as a proportion!
  
---
# Impact of Variable Scale: Y

Let's test this first re-scaling $Y$ in two ways in the .hi-red[multiple predictor case]:

1. Re-scale our dependent variable in millions of dollars in GDP (instead of dollars)
1. Standardize our dependent variable

---
# Re-scale GDP in Millions

```{r}
deu <- mutate(deu, 
              gdp_m = gdp/1000000, #<<
              gdp_z = (gdp - mean(gdp, na.rm = T))/sd(gdp, na.rm = T)) #<<
```

---
# Impact of Variable Scale

Generate predictors exactly as before:

.pull-left[
```{r}
synth_m <- synthetic_control(deu, 
      outcome = gdp_m, #<<
      unit = country, 
      time = year, 
      i_unit = "West Germany",
      i_time = 1990, 
      generate_placebos = F
    ) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1981:1990, 
                     gdp_81_90 = mean(gdp, na.rm = T),
                     trade_81_90 = mean(trade, na.rm = T), 
                     infrate_81_90 = mean(infrate, na.rm = T)
  ) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1971:1980, 
                     industry_71_80 = mean(industry, na.rm = T)) %>% 
  generate_predictor(time_window =c(1970, 1975), #<<
                     schooling_70_75 = mean(schooling, na.rm = T)) %>% #<<
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1980,
                     invest_80 = invest80)
```
].pull-right[
```{r}
synth_z <- synthetic_control(deu, 
      outcome = gdp_z, #<<
      unit = country, 
      time = year, 
      i_unit = "West Germany",
      i_time = 1990, 
      generate_placebos = F
    ) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1981:1990, 
                     gdp_81_90 = mean(gdp, na.rm = T),
                     trade_81_90 = mean(trade, na.rm = T), 
                     infrate_81_90 = mean(infrate, na.rm = T)
  ) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1971:1980, 
                     industry_71_80 = mean(industry, na.rm = T)) %>% 
  generate_predictor(time_window =c(1970, 1975), #<<
                     schooling_70_75 = mean(schooling, na.rm = T)) %>% #<<
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1980, 
                     invest_80 = invest80)
``` 
]

# Impact of Variable Scale

Estimate each model exactly as before:

.pull-left[
```{r}
synth_m <-   generate_weights(synth_m, 
                              optimization_window = 1981:1990) %>%
  generate_control()
```
].pull-right[
```{r}
synth_z <-   generate_weights(synth_z, 
                              optimization_window = 1981:1990) %>%
  generate_control()
```
]

---
# Comparing: Unit Weights

Comparing the unit weights:

```{r, echo = F}
# Unit weights
comp_unit <- grab_unit_weights(sc_81_90) %>%
  rename(Main = weight)
comp_unit_m <- grab_unit_weights(synth_m) %>%
  rename("Y Rescaled" = weight)
comp_unit_z <- grab_unit_weights(synth_z) %>%
  rename("Y Standardized" = weight)

left_join(comp_unit, comp_unit_m) %>%
  left_join(comp_unit_z) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) %>%
  arrange(desc(Main))
```
---
# Comparing: Predictor Weights

Comparing the predictor weights:

```{r, echo = F}
# Time weights
comp_pred <- grab_predictor_weights(sc_81_90) %>%
  rename(Main = weight)
comp_pred_m <- grab_predictor_weights(synth_m) %>%
  rename("Y Rescaled" = weight)
comp_pred_z <- grab_predictor_weights(synth_z) %>%
  rename("Y Standardized" = weight)

left_join(comp_pred, comp_pred_m) %>%
  left_join(comp_pred_z) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) %>%
  arrange(desc(Main))
```

# Rescale X

... huh. 

Okay... well What if we rescaled one of our $X$'s instead? Say, inflation rate as a percent?

```{r}
deu <- mutate(deu, inf_pct = infrate*100)
```
.font90[
```{r}
synth_x <- synthetic_control(deu, 
      outcome = gdp, 
      unit = country, 
      time = year, 
      i_unit = "West Germany",
      i_time = 1990, 
      generate_placebos = F
    ) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1981:1990, 
                     gdp_81_90 = mean(gdp, na.rm = T),
                     trade_81_90 = mean(trade, na.rm = T), 
                     infrate_81_90 = mean(inf_pct, na.rm = T) #<<
  ) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1971:1980, 
                     industry_71_80 = mean(industry, na.rm = T)) %>% 
  generate_predictor(time_window =c(1970, 1975), #<<
                     schooling_70_75 = mean(schooling, na.rm = T)) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1980,
                     invest_80 = invest80)

synth_x <-   generate_weights(synth_x, 
                              optimization_window = 1981:1990) %>%
  generate_control()
```
]
```{r, echo = F}
# Unit weights
comp_unit_x <- grab_unit_weights(synth_x) %>%
  rename("X Rescaled" = weight)

left_join(comp_unit, comp_unit_m) %>%
  left_join(comp_unit_x) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) %>%
  arrange(desc(Main))
```

---
# Rescale X

```{r, echo = F}
# Predictor weights
comp_pred_x <- grab_predictor_weights(synth_x) %>%
  rename("X Rescaled" = weight)

left_join(comp_pred, comp_pred_m) %>%
  left_join(comp_pred_x) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) %>%
  arrange(desc(Main))
```




---
# Rescale X

Wait, what?

--

It turns out that, while the standard SCM algorithm *isn't* X/Y scale-invariant,  .hi-slate[tidysynth] methods *are*. 

Looking into its [source code on Github](https://github.com/edunford/tidysynth/blob/58eda583ea28645a3531cd769b7852ff504656df/R/synth.R#L191) reveals why: it .hi-medgrn[internally standardizes all variables!]



---
# Punchline

* Synthetic control .hi-medgrn[is invariant to units/linear scaling of Y] but .hi-red[only when Y is the sole predictor]
* Canonical synthetic control .hi-red[is not invariant to units/linear scaling of Y/X with multiple predictors] 
  * Good idea to standardize your predictors *before* estimation
* .hi-slate[tidysynth] methods .hi-medgrn[internally standardize] all predictors and .hi-medgrn[are invariant to units/linear scaling of Y/X]
  * No need to pre-standardize!
